lead: Decentralization means moving control of a system from one authority to many participants. It exists because a single owner can fail, censor, or charge rent. Blockchain is one route: it replicates data, shares validation, and records rules in code. It is not the only route and not always the right one. You meet the idea in UPI-style payment switches, branch banking, supply chains, and decentralized applications. The useful distinctions are centralization, decentralization, and distribution. The useful questions are who writes, who validates, and who can change the rules.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2 for replicated databases and shared ledgers.

blocks.text: A centralized system has one node or office that controls writes and validation. Other nodes may hold read-only copies. A decentralized system has many participants sharing control; no single participant can change the accepted state alone. A distributed system spreads computation or storage across many machines.

Distribution is about where processing sits. Decentralization is about who controls writes and validation. A bank with one core server and 6 read-only branch databases is centralized and distributed. A service on 100 cloud machines run by one company is still centralized if that company alone writes and validates.

Partial decentralization shares some control but keeps a central owner for membership, identity, or upgrades. Full decentralization has no central operator. Most real systems are partial. The figure shows the common route.

sections.h3: Why decentralize, and what it costs

items: Single point of failure: one server or one administrator can fail or be attacked.
Censorship: a central owner can block a transaction, account, or application.
Trust: users need not trust one record keeper if many independent validators check the same ledger.
Cost: disintermediation removes a middle party and its fees.
Transparency: shared records can be audited by participants.
Coordination: many validators must agree; this takes messages and time.
Speed: shared validation is slower than one database write.
Governance: who changes the rules? Forks and votes are hard.
Legal clarity: responsibility is split across participants.

blocks.text: Decentralization is a trade, not a free upgrade. Use it when the failure, censorship, or trust cost of a central owner is higher than the coordination cost. A branch network may decentralize validation but keep central membership control. In a metaverse, shared asset records can let a user carry items between worlds; in payments, shared validation can reduce one switch's control.

items: Disintermediation: remove the middle party; buyer and seller deal directly.
Open participation: anyone may read, write, or validate under published rules.
Replicated data: every node keeps a copy of the ledger.
Shared validation: nodes agree on each write before it is accepted.
Token incentives: participants are paid or fined to follow the rules.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call these by other names; the mechanism is what matters. A common route has five steps: replicate the data across branches, open read access, open write access with signed transactions, add shared validation by consensus, then move rules into smart contracts. See Unit 3 for consensus and Unit 5 for smart contracts.

Smart contracts can hold escrow until delivery, send micropayments per use, or run a decentralized lottery without a central cashier. A DAO is a destination: an organization run by code and token votes, with no central boss. Decentralized applications (dApps) on Ethereum are another destination.

Blockchain alone does not give full ecosystem decentralization. If one company controls all validators, identity, and upgrades, the system is centralized in control even if it is distributed in storage. In practice, the decentralized web shares storage, identity, and naming; many projects still rely on central gateways.

figure.caption: The same 7 sites, 1 head office plus 6 branches, drawn twice. In the top row only the head office writes, so the write share is 1/7 ≈ 14.3% even though all 7 hold copies; in the bottom row all 7 validate, so the share is 7/7 = 100% with 7 ledger copies.

spec.title: 1 head office + 6 branches = 7 sites
spec.aria: Two rows of the same 7 sites: before, only the head office writes while the 6 branches hold read-only copies; after, all 7 sites validate writes on a shared ledger.

examples.question: A firm has 1 head-office server and 6 branch databases. The head office alone can write; branches hold read-only copies. Later all 6 branches and the head office validate writes on a shared ledger. (a) What fraction of the 7 sites can write before and after? (b) How many ledger copies exist after? (c) Is the first system centralized, decentralized, or distributed? (d) Which route did the firm take, and what may remain centralized?
steps: Count sites: 1 head office + 6 branches = 7 sites.
Before, writers = 1 (head office). Write share = 1/7 = 0.142857... ≈ 0.143, or 14.3%.
Before, all 7 sites hold copies, but only 1 writes. That is distributed storage with centralized control.
After, writers and validators = 7. Validation share = 7/7 = 1.0, or 100%.
Route: replicate to 7 sites, open writes to branches, add shared validation. Smart contracts and a DAO may come later.
Still centralized: head office may control membership, identity, or upgrade rules.
examples.answer: Before, 1/7 ≈ 0.143 (14.3%) of sites could write; after, 7/7 = 1.0 (100%) validate, with 7 copies. The first system is centralized but distributed; the route is replication plus shared validation, and membership or governance may remain central.
examples.check:
sites = 1 + 6
before_writers = 1
after_writers = 7
print(round(before_writers / sites, 3))
print(after_writers)
print(round(after_writers / sites, 3))

traps: "Many machines means decentralized" is wrong. Distribution is not control; one owner can run 100 machines and still be centralized.
"Distributed and decentralized are synonyms" is wrong. A distributed database can have one administrator who controls all writes.
"Blockchain always gives full decentralization" is wrong. The validator set, identity system, and upgrade rules can stay central.
"Decentralization has no cost" is wrong. Coordination, speed, governance, and legal clarity all become harder.
"A DAO has no rules" is wrong. A DAO has rules in code and token voting; it has no central boss, not no governance.

quiz.q: Define centralization, decentralization and distribution in one line each.
quiz.a: Centralization: one authority controls writes and validation. Decentralization: many participants share control of writes and validation. Distribution: computation or storage is spread across many machines.

quiz.q: Why can a service running on 100 cloud machines still be centralized?
quiz.a: If one company alone controls writes, validation, identity and upgrades, control is central even though the machines are spread out.

quiz.q: A firm has 1 writer and 9 read-only branches. What fraction of the 10 sites can write? After all 10 sites validate, what fraction validates?
quiz.a: Sites = 1 + 9 = 10. Before: 1/10 = 0.1 can write. After: 10/10 = 1.0 validate.

quiz.q: A blockchain has 20 nodes, but one company controls every validator and every software upgrade. Is it decentralized? Justify.
quiz.a: It is distributed in storage but centralized in control. The company can decide which blocks are accepted and which rules change, so participants do not share control.

quiz.q: Give two costs of decentralization and one reason it may still be worth paying them.
quiz.a: Costs: slower coordination and harder governance. It can be worth it when a central owner's failure, censorship or trust cost is higher than those coordination costs.

quiz.q: Match each method to its step: replicated data, shared validation, smart contracts. (a) every branch keeps a copy; (b) branches agree on each write; (c) rules run in code.
quiz.a: (a) replicated data; (b) shared validation; (c) smart contracts.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry work separates control decentralization from infrastructure distribution. Search for decentralized identity, consortium governance, and DAO governance attacks. Newer curricula add the decentralized web and data sovereignty. A useful question for any system is: who can write, who can validate, and who can change the rules?
